title: Twitter Timeline Design
description: Learn how Twitter designs its timeline service to handle hundreds of millions of users with the fan-out problem, push/pull models, and distributed caching.

data.text: Twitter's timeline is one of the most studied problems in system design. With over 450 million users generating hundreds of millions of tweets daily, the challenge is not just storing tweets — it is delivering the right tweets to the right users at the right time.

When a user posts a tweet, Twitter must decide how to deliver it to followers. A normal user with 500 followers requires 500 writes. A celebrity with 50 million followers requires 50 million writes. This asymmetry is the fan-out problem.

Twitter uses a hybrid approach. The push model writes tweets to follower timelines at post time. It works well for normal users but fails for celebrities. The pull model queries followee timelines at read time. It handles celebrities efficiently but increases read latency.

data.caption: Hybrid push/pull model for Twitter timeline generation

data.title: Hybrid Strategy
data.text: Twitter uses push for normal users and pull for celebrities. This hybrid approach keeps write costs manageable while avoiding read-time explosions for popular accounts.

The timeline service merges tweets from multiple sources: home timeline from push writes, user timelines from pull queries, and promoted tweets from an ad server. Each source is ranked by relevance before being merged.

rows: Immutable tweet storage with high write throughput
Pre-computed home timelines for fast reads

terms.definition: Distributing content from one source to many destinations; the core scaling challenge for timeline services.
Writing content to all consumer timelines at creation time; efficient for reads, expensive for popular creators.
Querying source timelines at read time; efficient for popular creators, expensive for reads.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Timeline generation is dominated by the fan-out problem
Hybrid push/pull models balance write and read costs
Pre-computed timelines in Redis enable sub-100ms reads
Relevance ranking happens after timeline assembly
data.takeaway: Timeline design teaches that one-size-fits-all scaling fails — identify workload patterns and use the right model for each.

data.title: Design a Timeline Service
data.description: Design a simplified timeline service for a social network with 100 million users. Normal users have 500 followers; 0.1% are celebrities with 10 million followers. Choose push, pull, or hybrid and justify your choice with capacity estimates.
data.expectedOutcome: Hybrid is optimal: push for normal users (500 writes per tweet) and pull for celebrities (query at read time). Estimate ~50 billion timeline writes per month for normal users.

items.question: How does Twitter handle deleted tweets in cached timelines?
items.answer: Tombstones are written to cached timelines. When a user reads their timeline, the tombstone filters the tweet. This is a write amplification trade-off.

items.question: Why does Twitter use multiple storage systems?
items.answer: Different access patterns need different storage. Tweets are append-only (Cassandra), timelines need low-latency reads (Redis), and social graphs need graph traversal (FlockDB).
